## Today {.unnumbered}

Some numbers rest on a lot of data, some on very little. Today we learn the
Bayesian way of taking that into account, first with restaurants and a well,
then with lung cancer in Pennsylvania. Reading: **Moraga Ch. 3, 4 and
§5.1--5.3**.

::: {.callout-note}
## By the end of today you can

1. explain *prior*, *data* and *posterior* with an everyday example;
2. explain why the SIR of a small county is unreliable;
3. say what *shrinkage* does, and to which counties;
4. read a smoothed map and an exceedance map made with R-INLA.
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| code-fold: false

library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(spdep)
library(SpatialEpi)   # pennLC
library(INLA)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
**Install INLA before class.** It is not on CRAN:

```r
install.packages("INLA",
  repos = c(getOption("repos"), INLA = "https://inla.r-inla-download.org/R/stable"))
```
:::

# The Bayesian idea in one example

## Two restaurants

| | Number of reviews | Average rating |
|---|---|---|
| Restaurant A | 2 | 5.0 ★ |
| Restaurant B | 800 | 4.7 ★ |

Which one would you pick? Most people pick B, even though A has the higher
average: two five-star reviews could come from the owner's friends. Without
noticing, you did three things.

1. You started from what you know about restaurants in general: a typical one
   gets about 4.0 stars. That is the **prior**.
2. You looked at each restaurant's own reviews. That is the **data**.
3. You combined the two, trusting the reviews more when there are many. That is
   the **posterior**, your best guess.

## The best guess is an average

Where does the prior come from? Recently, **10 people** tried restaurants in
the area, and their average rating was **4.0 stars**. We **borrow** these 10
ratings and add them to each restaurant's own reviews; the best guess is the
average of all the ratings, borrowed and own. With $n$ own reviews,

$$
\text{best guess} \;=\; \frac{\text{total stars}}{\text{total ratings}}
\;=\; \frac{10 \times 4.0 \;+\; n \times \text{its average}}{10 + n}.
$$

Two or three own reviews cannot overturn the 10 borrowed ratings; a few dozen
can. The same best guess is a weighted average,

$$
\text{best guess} \;=\; w \times \text{its average} \;+\; (1 - w) \times 4.0,
\qquad w = \frac{n}{n + 10},
$$

where $w$ is the **share of its own reviews**: how much we **trust its own
reviews**, between 0 and 1. In R:

```{r}
#| label: restaurants

best_guess <- function(reviews, average, prior_mean = 4.0, borrowed = 10) {
  w <- reviews / (reviews + borrowed)           # share of its own reviews
  w * average + (1 - w) * prior_mean            # weighted average
}

best_guess(reviews = 2,   average = 5.0)        # Restaurant A
best_guess(reviews = 800, average = 4.7)        # Restaurant B
```

Restaurant A's 5.0 is pulled back to `r round(best_guess(2, 5.0), 2)`: two
reviews are not enough to convince us. B barely moves, to
`r round(best_guess(800, 4.7), 2)`. Pulling an estimate toward the average is
called **shrinkage**.

## More reviews, less shrinkage

What if A kept getting five-star reviews?

```{r}
#| label: restaurants-more

tibble(reviews = c(1, 2, 5, 10, 50, 100, 800)) |>
  mutate(w          = round(reviews / (reviews + 10), 2),   # share of its own reviews
         best_guess = round(best_guess(reviews, 5.0), 2))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-restaurants
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-cap: "Best guess for a restaurant whose reviews all give 5.0 stars, as reviews accumulate."

tibble(reviews = 1:1000) |>
  mutate(guess = best_guess(reviews, 5.0)) |>
  ggplot(aes(reviews, guess)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(4, 5), linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = c(3.95, 5.05), hjust = 0, size = 3.5,
           label = c("prior: a typical restaurant (4.0)", "its own reviews (5.0)")) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, colour = "darkgreen") +
  geom_point(data = tibble(reviews = 2, guess = best_guess(2, 5.0)), size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.4, y = best_guess(2, 5.0), label = "Restaurant A",
           hjust = 0, vjust = 1.6, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Number of reviews (log scale)", y = "Best guess (stars)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

With 2 reviews, the guess stays close to the prior. With 10 own reviews, as
many as the borrowed ones, it sits exactly halfway. With hundreds, the prior hardly
matters.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key idea
The posterior is a compromise between the prior and the data. The more data,
the more the data win.
:::

# Learning one test at a time: is the well water safe?

## The story

A family tests its well for arsenic ten times. The EPA limit is 10 µg/L. Their
question: **how often is this water above the limit?** Call that share
$\theta$: $\theta = 0.2$ means unsafe one test in five.

```{r}
#| label: data-arsenic

epa   <- 10                                          # EPA limit, µg/L
conc  <- c(14, 7, 12, 18, 11, 15, 9, 13, 14, 14)     # 10 tests (illustrative)
above <- as.integer(conc > epa)                      # 1 = above, 0 = below
above
```

We do not start from nothing. In nearby wells, about **half** of past tests
were above the limit: 5 of 10. That is our **prior**, centred on
$\theta = 0.5$. A Beta curve keeps the score: Beta(5, 5) means 10 tests
borrowed from the neighbours, 5 above and 5 below. Each new test above the limit adds 1
to the first number, each test below adds 1 to the second.

## Watching the posterior learn

In each panel, red dotted is what we believed **before** the test, green is
what we believe **after**.

```{r}
#| label: fn-update
#| code-fold: true

plot_update <- function(a, b, x, n, title = "") {
  theta <- seq(0, 1, 0.001)
  plot(theta, dbeta(theta, a, b), type = "l", lty = 3, lwd = 3, col = "red",
       ylim = c(0, 4), bty = "l", xlab = expression(theta), ylab = "",
       main = title)                                            # before
  if (n > 0)                                                    # no test, no update
    lines(theta, dbeta(theta, a + x, b + n - x), lwd = 3, col = "darkgreen")  # after
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-seq-chain
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6.5
#| fig-cap: "Each panel starts from the previous panel's green curve and adds one test."

par(mfrow = c(3, 4), mar = c(4, 2, 2, 1))

a <- 5; b <- 5                                      # prior: 5 of 10 above in nearby wells
plot_update(a, b, 0, 0, title = "Before testing: nearby wells")

for (i in 1:10) {
  plot_update(a, b, above[i], 1,
              title = paste0("#", i, ": ", conc[i], " ug/L",
                             ifelse(above[i] == 1, " (above)", " (below)")))
  a <- a + above[i]                                 # after ...
  b <- b + 1 - above[i]                             # ... becomes next before
}
```

Three things to notice:

1. A test above the limit pushes the curve right; a test below pushes it left
   (tests 2 and 7).
2. The curve gets **taller and narrower**: more tests, more certainty.
3. Each panel's green curve becomes the next panel's red curve. That is
   Bayesian learning.

::: {.callout-note}
**Why does the y-axis stop at 4?** It shows a density, not a probability, so
it can exceed 1; the area under each curve is 1. We fix it at 4 so the panels
can be compared.
:::

## What do we know after ten tests?

```{r}
#| label: read-post

a / (a + b)                                      # best guess for θ
qbeta(c(0.025, 0.975), a, b)                     # 95% credible interval
1 - pbeta(0.5, a, b)                             # P(unsafe more than half the time)
```

Our best guess is that the water is above the limit about
`r round(100 * a / (a + b))`% of the time, and with 95% probability between
`r round(100 * qbeta(0.025, a, b))`% and `r round(100 * qbeta(0.975, a, b))`%
(the **credible interval**). The probability that it is unsafe more than half
the time is `r sprintf("%.2f", 1 - pbeta(0.5, a, b))`. Bayesian results answer
the family's question directly, as a probability.

Where does `r round(100 * a / (a + b))`% come from? The well's own tests say
`r sum(above)` of 10, `r round(100 * mean(above))`%. The nearby wells say 50%.
The 10 borrowed tests and the well's own 10 count equally, so the answer sits
halfway. It is the restaurant formula again:

$$
`r sprintf("%.2f", a / (a + b))` \;=\; w \times `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(above))`
\;+\; (1 - w) \times 0.50,
\qquad w = \frac{10}{10 + 10} = 0.5.
$$

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key idea
We start from what we already know, here the nearby wells, and each new test
updates it. More data, a narrower curve, more certainty.
:::

# Counties: why small counties need help

## The data

We rebuild the Pennsylvania lung cancer counts from the SIR lecture: $O$
observed cases, $E$ expected cases, and SIR $= O/E$.

```{r}
#| label: recap
#| code-fold: true

data(pennLC)
d <- pennLC$data

ref <- d |>
  group_by(race, gender, age) |>
  summarise(r = sum(cases) / sum(population), .groups = "drop")   # reference rates

county <- d |>
  left_join(ref, by = c("race", "gender", "age")) |>
  group_by(county) |>
  summarise(O = sum(cases), E = sum(population * r), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(county = as.character(county), SIR = O / E)

pa <- st_as_sf(pennLC$spatial.polygon) |>
  st_set_crs(4326) |>
  mutate(county = names(pennLC$spatial.polygon)) |>
  st_transform(5070) |>                                           # Albers
  left_join(county, by = "county")

sir_breaks <- c(0, 0.67, 0.83, 0.95, 1.05, 1.2, 1.5, Inf)
sir_fill   <- scale_fill_brewer(palette = "RdBu", direction = -1, drop = FALSE, name = "Risk")
```

## The SIR map

```{r}
#| label: fig-sir
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-cap: "Lung cancer SIRs, Pennsylvania counties."

ggplot(pa) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = cut(SIR, sir_breaks)), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  sir_fill +
  theme_void(base_size = 12)
```

Which counties have the most extreme SIRs?

```{r}
#| label: sir-extremes

extremes <- county |>
  arrange(SIR) |>
  slice(c(1:3, 65:67)) |>                           # 3 lowest, 3 highest
  mutate(E = round(E, 1), SIR = round(SIR, 2))
extremes
```

Of these six counties, `r sum(extremes$E < 20)` expect fewer than 20 cases;
the median county expects `r round(median(county$E))`. A few cases more or less
move their SIR a lot. Small counties are like restaurants with two reviews.

## The funnel plot

How far can an SIR stray by chance alone? If a county's true risk were exactly
the state's, its SIR would still fall, about 95% of the time, within
$1 \pm 1.96/\sqrt{E}$. Plotted against $E$, that range is a funnel.

```{r}
#| label: fig-funnel
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "SIRs against expected cases. Grey: where about 95% of SIRs fall by chance alone."

funnel <- tibble(E = exp(seq(log(4), log(1500), length.out = 200))) |>
  mutate(lo = 1 - 1.96 / sqrt(E),                   # chance range of the SIR
         hi = 1 + 1.96 / sqrt(E))

labelled <- filter(county, county %in% c("sullivan", "potter", "juniata", "philadelphia"))

ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = funnel, aes(E, ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "grey85") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(data = county, aes(E, SIR)) +
  geom_text(data = labelled, aes(E, SIR, label = tools::toTitleCase(county)),
            nudge_y = 0.07, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Expected cases (log scale)", y = "SIR") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The funnel is wide on the left. Potter's 1.37 and Sullivan's 0.40 sit inside
it: they could be chance. Philadelphia's 1.16 is far outside: with more than
1,200 expected cases, a 16% excess is not chance.

::: {.callout-important}
## The problem in one sentence
A raw SIR mixes real differences in risk with chance, and chance is largest in
small counties.
:::

# Shrinkage: the restaurant formula for counties

## Same formula, new names

| Restaurants | Counties |
|---|---|
| number of reviews | expected cases $E$ |
| its average rating | its SIR |
| a typical restaurant, 4.0 | the state average, 1 |
| 10 borrowed ratings, average 4.0 | $k$ borrowed expected cases at the state rate |
| trust in its own reviews, $w$ | trust in its own SIR, $w$ |

So each county gets

$$
\text{estimate} \;=\; w \times \text{SIR} \;+\; (1 - w) \times 1,
\qquad w = \frac{E}{E + k}.
$$

A big county (large $E$) keeps its SIR. A small county borrows from the state.

## Who decides $k$? The data

For the restaurants we picked 10 ourselves. For counties, R estimates $k$ from
the 67 SIRs:

- if counties differ **much more** than chance alone would produce, real
  differences are large, we trust each county's SIR, and $k$ is small;
- if counties differ **about as much** as chance would produce, we trust the
  state average more, and $k$ is large.

Letting the data choose the prior this way is called **empirical Bayes**
(Clayton and Kaldor 1987; Marshall 1991). `EBest()` in **spdep** does it in
one line.

```{r}
#| label: eb-global

eb <- EBest(pa$O, pa$E)                              # cases, expected cases
pa$RR_eb <- eb$estmm                                 # shrunk estimate

k <- with(attr(eb, "parameters"), b / a)             # k borrowed expected cases
k
pa$w <- pa$E / (pa$E + k)                            # trust in own SIR
```

Each county borrows about `r round(k)` expected cases at the state rate. Here are five
counties, from small to large:

```{r}
#| label: eb-table

pa |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(county %in% c("sullivan", "potter", "venango", "lehigh", "philadelphia")) |>
  arrange(E) |>
  transmute(county, E = round(E), SIR = round(SIR, 2),
            w = round(w, 2), estimate = round(RR_eb, 2))
```

Sullivan's own 7 expected cases are mixed with `r round(k)` borrowed ones: we
trust its SIR
only `r round(100 * pa$w[pa$county == "sullivan"])`%, and its estimate is
almost the state's. Philadelphia, with more than 1,200 expected cases, keeps
`r round(100 * pa$w[pa$county == "philadelphia"])`% of its SIR. Potter and
Venango have the same SIR, 1.37, like two restaurants with the same average,
but Venango rests on three times more cases, so it stays higher:
`r sprintf("%.2f", pa$RR_eb[pa$county == "venango"])` against
`r sprintf("%.2f", pa$RR_eb[pa$county == "potter"])`.

## Where do we borrow?

```{r}
#| label: fig-weights
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-cap: "Trust in each county's own SIR. Dark: we keep the county's SIR. Light: we borrow from the state."

ggplot(pa) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = w), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Purples", direction = 1, limits = c(0, 1),
                       name = "Trust w") +
  theme_void(base_size = 12)
```

The map of $w$ is a map of population: the rural north and centre borrow the
most, the Philadelphia and Pittsburgh areas the least.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key idea
Small counties borrow from the state; big counties keep their own SIR. The
data decide how much to borrow.
:::

# Full Bayes with R-INLA

Empirical Bayes gives one number per county. A **full Bayesian** model does the
same shrinkage but returns a whole posterior curve per county, like the green
curves of the well. That tells us **how sure** we are. INLA is a fast way to
fit such models (Moraga Ch. 3--4).

We use the **BYM2** model (Moraga §5.3). Instead of borrowing from the whole
state, each county borrows mostly from its **neighbours**, the way the family
borrowed from nearby wells. We use the queen neighbours from the Moran's I
lecture.

```{r}
#| label: m2

dat <- st_drop_geometry(pa) |>
  mutate(id = row_number())                          # one index per county

nb <- poly2nb(pa, queen = TRUE)                      # queen neighbours
nb2INLA("pa.adj", nb)                                # write for INLA
g  <- inla.read.graph("pa.adj")

m2 <- inla(O ~ 1 + f(id, model = "bym2", graph = g),
           family = "poisson", E = E, data = dat,
           control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
           control.compute = list(return.marginals.predictor = TRUE))

dat$RR_bym2 <- m2$summary.fitted.values$mean         # posterior mean risk
```

Read the formula as: log-risk = an overall level + a bump for each county that
borrows from its neighbours (Moraga §4.1).

## How does INLA get a credible interval?

For every county, INLA returns a whole **posterior curve** for its relative
risk, like the green curves of the well. For the well, a simple formula gave
the curve. Here it cannot, because each county borrows from its neighbours,
and we do not know **how much** to borrow: that depends on how different the
counties really are, which is itself unknown. INLA works in three steps
(Moraga §3.2):

1. **Try several amounts of borrowing.** For each plausible value of how much
   the counties differ, it computes the county's curve with a fast bell-shaped
   (Laplace) approximation.
2. **Average the curves.** It weights each curve by how well that amount of
   borrowing fits all 67 counties, and averages them. This is the
   *integrated* in INLA.
3. **Read the final curve.** The posterior mean is its balance point; the 95%
   credible interval cuts 2.5% of the area off each side; the exceedance
   probability is the area to the right of 1.

Here are steps 1 and 2 for Potter. Each dashed curve fixes one amount of
borrowing, from little to a lot; the thick grey curve is INLA's final curve.

```{r}
#| label: fig-inla-steps
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-cap: "Potter County. Dashed: posterior curves for three fixed amounts of borrowing. Thick grey: INLA's final curve, which averages over all plausible amounts."

k   <- which(dat$county == "potter")
tau <- c(10, m2$summary.hyperpar["Precision for id", "0.5quant"], 1000)   # little, middle, a lot
phi <- m2$summary.hyperpar["Phi for id", "0.5quant"]

fixed_fit <- function(t) {                           # BYM2 with borrowing fixed
  hyp <- list(prec = list(initial = log(t),   fixed = TRUE),
              phi  = list(initial = qlogis(phi), fixed = TRUE))
  m <- inla(O ~ 1 + f(id, model = "bym2", graph = g, hyper = hyp),
            family = "poisson", E = E, data = dat,
            control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
            control.compute = list(return.marginals.predictor = TRUE))
  inla.smarginal(m$marginals.fitted.values[[k]])     # Potter's curve
}

lab <- c("borrow little (counties very different)", "borrow a middle amount",
         "borrow a lot (counties very similar)")
steps <- bind_rows(lapply(1:3, function(j) data.frame(fixed_fit(tau[j]), curve = lab[j]))) |>
  mutate(curve = factor(curve, lab))
final <- data.frame(inla.smarginal(m2$marginals.fitted.values[[k]]))

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = final, aes(x, y), linewidth = 2.5, alpha = 0.35) +     # final curve, underneath
  geom_line(data = steps, aes(x, y, colour = curve), linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = dat$SIR[k], linetype = 3, colour = "blue") +
  annotate("text", x = dat$SIR[k], y = 0, label = " Potter's SIR", hjust = 0,
           vjust = -0.5, colour = "blue", size = 3.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#D95F02", "#7570B3", "#1B9E77"), name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.5, 1.8)) +
  labs(x = "Relative risk, Potter", y = "Posterior density") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.direction = "vertical")
```

Borrowing little leaves Potter closer to its own SIR, with a wide curve;
borrowing a lot pulls it toward its neighbours, with a narrow curve. The data
make the middle amount the most plausible, so the final curve sits close to
it. Step 3 then reads the
answers off the final curve:

```{r}
#| label: fig-read-curve
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Potter's final posterior curve. Left: the 95% credible interval leaves 2.5% of the area in each grey tail. Right: the exceedance probability is the red area to the right of 1."

LL <- m2$summary.fitted.values$`0.025quant`[k]
UL <- m2$summary.fitted.values$`0.975quant`[k]
P1 <- 1 - inla.pmarginal(1, m2$marginals.fitted.values[[k]])

p_ci <- ggplot(final, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(data = filter(final, x <= LL), fill = "grey70") +
  geom_area(data = filter(final, x >= UL), fill = "grey70") +
  geom_line(colour = "darkgreen", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(LL, UL), linetype = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = UL + 0.04, y = max(final$y) * 0.6, size = 3.5, hjust = 0,
           label = paste0("95% credible interval\n", sprintf("%.2f", LL),
                          " to ", sprintf("%.2f", UL))) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.5, 1.8)) +
  labs(title = "Credible interval", x = "Relative risk, Potter", y = "Posterior density") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)

p_exc <- ggplot(final, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(data = filter(final, x >= 1), fill = "#d7191c", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(colour = "darkgreen", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.35, y = max(final$y) * 0.6, size = 3.5,
           label = paste0("P(risk > 1) = ", sprintf("%.2f", P1))) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.5, 1.8)) +
  labs(title = "Exceedance probability", x = "Relative risk, Potter", y = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)

p_ci + p_exc
```

In R, the same numbers come straight from the curve:

```{r}
#| label: read-curve

marg <- m2$marginals.fitted.values[[k]]          # Potter's posterior curve
inla.qmarginal(c(0.025, 0.975), marg)            # 95% credible interval
1 - inla.pmarginal(1, marg)                      # P(risk > 1)
```

## Three maps

```{r}
#| label: fig-maps
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Raw SIR, empirical Bayes and BYM2. Same colours."

pa |>
  select(county) |>
  left_join(select(dat, county, SIR, RR_eb, RR_bym2), by = "county") |>
  pivot_longer(c(SIR, RR_eb, RR_bym2), names_to = "estimate", values_to = "risk") |>
  mutate(estimate = factor(estimate, c("SIR", "RR_eb", "RR_bym2"),
                           c("SIR (raw)", "Empirical Bayes", "BYM2 (INLA)"))) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = cut(risk, sir_breaks)), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  facet_wrap(~ estimate) +
  sir_fill +
  theme_void(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The extreme colours of the raw map, mostly small rural counties, fade. What
remains is the broad pattern.

## How sure are we? The exceedance map

For the well we asked: how likely is it that the water is unsafe more than half
the time? For each county we ask: how likely is it that its risk is above the
state average, $P(\theta > 1)$? This is the **exceedance probability**. It
is the red area of the figure above, computed for every county.

```{r}
#| label: exceed

dat$p_exc <- sapply(m2$marginals.fitted.values,
                    function(m) 1 - inla.pmarginal(1, m))   # P(θ > 1)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-exceed
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-cap: "Probability that each county's lung cancer risk exceeds the state average (BYM2)."

exc_cols <- c("Probably lower (< 0.2)"  = "#2c7bb6",
              "Uncertain (0.2–0.8)"     = "grey90",
              "Probably higher (> 0.8)" = "#d7191c")

pa |>
  select(county) |>
  left_join(select(dat, county, p_exc), by = "county") |>
  mutate(exc = cut(p_exc, c(0, 0.2, 0.8, 1), labels = names(exc_cols),
                   include.lowest = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = exc), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = exc_cols, drop = FALSE, name = NULL) +
  theme_void(base_size = 12)
```

Counties probably above average:
`r paste(tools::toTitleCase(dat$county[dat$p_exc > 0.8]), collapse = ", ")`.
Potter, despite its SIR of 1.37, is not among them
($P = `r sprintf("%.2f", dat$p_exc[dat$county == "potter"])`$): 22 cases are
not enough.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key idea
INLA does the same shrinkage, borrows from the neighbours, and tells us how
sure we are about each county.
:::

# In-class exercise {.unnumbered}

Work in pairs, 15 minutes.

1. **Restaurants.** Suppose 100 people, not 10, had tried restaurants in the
   area. Run `best_guess(2, 5.0, borrowed = 100)` and
   `best_guess(800, 4.7, borrowed = 100)`. What happens to A and to B? Why?
2. **Well water.** Suppose the family knew nothing about nearby wells and
   started from a flat prior, `a <- 1; b <- 1`. Rerun the updating. How does
   the final best guess change, and why?
3. **Funnel.** Cameron County has an SIR of
   `r sprintf("%.2f", county$SIR[county$county == "cameron"])` with only
   `r round(county$E[county$county == "cameron"])` expected cases. Is it inside
   the funnel? What is its empirical Bayes estimate,
   `pa$RR_eb[pa$county == "cameron"]`? Explain the difference.
4. **Interpretation.** In two sentences for a county health officer, explain
   why Potter is not flagged even though its SIR is 1.37.

# Key takeaways {.unnumbered}

1. The posterior is a compromise between the prior and the data; the more
   data, the more the data win.
2. A raw SIR mixes real differences and chance; chance is largest in small
   counties.
3. Shrinkage: small counties borrow from the state (or their neighbours), big
   counties keep their SIR.
4. Report how sure we are, not only the estimate: exceedance probabilities.

# Words to know {.unnumbered}

| Word | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| Prior | what we believe before seeing the data |
| Likelihood | what the data say |
| Posterior | what we believe after seeing the data |
| Credible interval | a range that contains the true value with 95% probability |
| Shrinkage | pulling unreliable estimates toward an average |
| Empirical Bayes | shrinkage where the data decide how much to shrink |
| Exceedance probability | the probability that a risk is above a threshold, e.g. the state average |
